name: Epicatechin

lead: Epicatechin is promoted to lifters as a way to lower myostatin, the brake on muscle growth, for extra muscle mass. It is a flavan-3-ol, a plant polyphenol found in cocoa, green tea, apples and berries.

Proponents say it lowers myostatin and raises follistatin. That theory comes mainly from a small open-label pilot in seven men with Becker muscular dystrophy, where biopsies showed higher follistatin and lower myostatin after eight weeks, plus animal work. Controlled trials in healthy lifters were not found. Other human work examines blood vessel function.

paras: It is sold as capsules or in cocoa-extract products and taken daily, often alongside a training program and other muscle supplements.
Acute toxicity is low in rodents, and mild GI effects are reported at higher catechin intakes. Other catechins such as green tea extract have liver safety concerns.

angle.text: Promoted to lifters as a myostatin inhibitor that could allow extra muscle growth from a cocoa flavanol. The evidence is a small pilot in seven muscular dystrophy patients and animal work, not trials in lifters.

lead: (-)-Epicatechin is a flavan-3-ol, a type of plant polyphenol found in cocoa, green tea, apples and berries [1][2]. As a supplement it is promoted for muscle growth on the theory that it lowers myostatin and raises follistatin.

That theory comes mainly from a small open-label pilot in seven men with Becker muscular dystrophy, in which muscle biopsies showed higher follistatin and lower myostatin after eight weeks [2]. Controlled trials in healthy lifters were not found; the Wikipedia catechin article does not discuss muscle effects at all [1]. Other human work examines blood vessel function, and epicatechin trials in muscular dystrophy are small [2].

paras: Epicatechin is the cis form of catechin, with two chiral centres; (-)-epicatechin is the common natural isomer [1][2]. Wikipedia reports cocoa as the richest food source analysed in catechin terms [1]. Grokipedia gives figures such as about 41 to 70 mg per 100 g in dark chocolate and about 6 to 8 mg per 100 ml in brewed green tea [2]. Uptake is highest for (-)-epicatechin among catechin forms, and most dietary catechins are broken down by gut bacteria [1].

Grokipedia describes an eight-week pilot in seven adult men with Becker muscular dystrophy, in which biopsies showed more mitochondrial and regeneration markers, higher follistatin and lower myostatin [2]. Animal work in dystrophy models and aged mice is also cited [2]. These were patients, not healthy lifters, and there was no control group in the pilot.

Grokipedia states that acute toxicity is low in rodents and that mild gastrointestinal effects have been reported with catechin intakes above about 500 mg a day, drawn from studies of related catechins [2]. Wikipedia notes that green tea extract catechins can be hepatotoxic, that EFSA recommends supplements not exceed 800 mg a day of catechins, and that a catechin drug, Catergen, was withdrawn in 1985 after autoimmune haemolytic anaemia [1].

Registered trials include Becker muscular dystrophy studies [3][4], a Duchenne muscular dystrophy study [5], Friedreich's ataxia [6] and a pre-diabetes pharmacology study [7]. A meta-analysis of cocoa flavanol trials reported small blood-pressure reductions, and a 20-man crossover found improved flow-mediated dilation [2]. A trial in obese adults gave no significant change in body measures over 12 weeks [2]. Limits include small samples and short durations [2].
